name: Erythromycin (acne)

card.summary: A prescription macrolide antibiotic solution for acne, usually paired with benzoyl peroxide because acne bacteria can become resistant.
card.note: Often combined with benzoyl peroxide to limit antibiotic resistance.

quick.overview:
Topical erythromycin 2% is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. Reference sources describe it as a mild-to-moderate acne option, typically combined with benzoyl peroxide.

It is a long-established antibiotic, introduced in 1952.
quick.mechanism: It binds the bacterial ribosome and stops protein synthesis, reducing acne-associated bacteria.
quick.risks: Local dryness, peeling, itching, redness; rare hives. Labels warn of antibiotic-associated colitis. Reference sources note it is usually paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit resistance.

lead: Topical erythromycin is a prescription antibiotic applied to the skin to calm inflamed acne, the red papules and pustules that dominate the look of breakouts. By reducing acne-associated bacteria, it helps lessen active spots and the redness around them, so skin looks clearer and evener over time. It is a macrolide antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein synthesis, and a 2% topical solution is labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. [1][2][3]

Dermatology guidance describes topical antibiotics, erythromycin among them, as most often paired with benzoyl peroxide, which limits the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. [1][4][5] The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline as part of acne care. [4] Wikipedia notes that resistance to topical macrolides such as erythromycin has risen worldwide with broad antibiotic use. [5]

Preventing breakouts matters for appearance beyond the spots themselves: Wikipedia reports that acne scarring is estimated to affect most people with acne, and that post-inflammatory darkening can persist for months or years in people with darker skin. [5] Erythromycin has been on the market since 1952. [2]

chain: Fewer acne-associated bacteria and less inflammation
Fewer red, inflamed spots and less risk of marks
angle.text: People use topical erythromycin, usually with benzoyl peroxide, to reduce inflamed pimples so skin looks clearer and calmer. Fewer active lesions also means fewer opportunities for lasting marks and scars.

infobox: Prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia [2]

paras: The US label for erythromycin topical solution 2% lists acne vulgaris as its indication. [3] Grokipedia describes it as used for mild to moderate inflammatory acne, usually combined with benzoyl peroxide. [1] Wikipedia lists erythromycin alongside clindamycin, metronidazole and sulfacetamide as topical antibiotics for mild to moderately severe acne, and says dermatologists prefer to use antibiotics in combination rather than alone. [5]

On T Nation, users discussing hormone-related breakouts have mentioned a prescription routine of benzoyl peroxide wash followed by an erythromycin pad, and another poster listed erythromycin among antibiotics that worked for friends but not for them. [6][7]

sections.h: Combination with benzoyl peroxide and resistance
paras: Wikipedia states that benzoyl peroxide does not appear to cause bacterial resistance, unlike antibiotics, and that pairing the two is common in dermatology. [5] The same article says topical and oral antibiotics should not be used together, and that long oral courses are paired with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid. [5] The 2024 AAD guideline provides the evidence-based framework for these recommendations. [4]

The label lists occasional local reactions: peeling, dryness, itching, erythema and oiliness, with eye irritation and skin tenderness also reported. [3] Urticarial reactions requiring steroid treatment have been reported. [3] The label carries a warning about pseudomembranous colitis, which has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents. [3] It lists pregnancy category B, noting no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women. [3]
Erythromycin binds the 50S bacterial ribosomal subunit and halts protein synthesis; its effect is mainly bacteriostatic. [1][2]
Erythromycin was launched as Ilosone by Eli Lilly in 1952 and patented the following year. [2]

The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline, a systematic review with graded recommendations, strongly recommends topical antibiotics for acne, alongside benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids and oral doxycycline. [4] Other trials of erythromycin in the literature concern non-acne conditions such as gastrointestinal and obstetric uses.

timeline.event: Erythromycin launched as Ilosone by Eli Lilly. [2]

lore.intro: Erythromycin for acne appears only in passing in forum discussions of acne treatments on T Nation. [6][7]

claims.claim: An erythromycin pad plus benzoyl peroxide wash is a prescription routine for stubborn breakouts.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster suggested getting a benzoyl peroxide wash prescribed and following it with an erythromycin pad. [6]
claims.experts: Guidelines describe topical antibiotics combined with benzoyl peroxide as a recommended approach. [4][5]
